claims.evidence: Supported by video observations of JMP morphology.

claims.claim: Long-term TNFα treatment (20 hr) increases the overall volume of JMPs.
claims.source: These data revealed that short-term, that is, 4 hr (not shown), and long-term TNFα treatment, that is, 20 hr, to the same extend increased the overall volume of the JMPs as well as the dynamics of these JMPs, as well as the area of the JMP on the endothelium, although the latter one was not significant (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E-F using LLSM imaging and automated analysis.

claims.claim: TNFα treatment increases the dynamics of JMPs.
claims.source: These data revealed that short-term, that is, 4 hr (not shown), and long-term TNFα treatment, that is, 20 hr, to the same extend increased the overall volume of the JMPs as well as the dynamics of these JMPs, as well as the area of the JMP on the endothelium, although the latter one was not significant (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E-F demonstrating increased fluctuations in JMP volume over time.

claims.claim: JMPs colocalize with VE-cadherin.
claims.source: Figure 1G shows an example of such a JMP dynamics in time map and showed that JMPs colocalized with VE-cadherin (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data showing colocalization in Figure 1G-H.

claims.claim: All inflammatory stimuli tested (TNFα, LPS, IFNγ, and IL1β) show the same JMP dynamics.
claims.source: We additionally checked if other inflammatory stimuli, that is, LPS, INFγ, and IL1β, changed the dynamic rate of JMPs compared to TNFα. Using the simplified algorithm to generate a membrane dynamics map, we quantified JMPs by simply taking the mean value of this image (for details see Materials and methods section). We found that all inflammatory stimuli tested showed the same JMP dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing different inflammatory stimuli shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: JMP dynamics do not differ in endothelial cells isolated from different origins.
claims.source: Also, when we tested JMP dynamics in endothelial cells that were isolated from different origin, we did not find differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing endothelial cells from different origins shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Short-term flow (5 or 20 min) increases JMP activity.
claims.source: Indeed, short-term flow for 5 or 20 min did increase JMP activity, whereas exposure of the endothelial cells to longer periods of flow, that is, 30–60 min, reduced JMP dynamics back to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased JMP dynamics with short-term flow in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Longer periods of flow (30-60 min) reduce JMP dynamics back to basal levels.
claims.source: Indeed, short-term flow for 5 or 20 min did increase JMP activity, whereas exposure of the endothelial cells to longer periods of flow, that is, 30–60 min, reduced JMP dynamics back to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics with longer flow exposure in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: There is no preference of JMP dynamics at the upstream or downstream side of the flow direction.
claims.source: We did not find any preference of JMP dynamics at the upstream or downstream side of the flow direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing upstream and downstream JMP dynamics in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Inflammatory stimuli promote the dynamics but not the actual appearance or size of JMPs.
claims.source: Thus, these data show that inflammatory stimuli promote the dynamics but not the actual appearance or size of JMPs.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments testing different inflammatory stimuli and their effects on JMP characteristics.

claims.claim: Most neutrophils prefer exit-sites with high-membrane activity.
claims.source: To investigate this, mNeonGreen-CAAX transduced HUVECs were used to study neutrophil TEM under flow conditions. We found that most neutrophils preferred exit-sites with high-membrane activity (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations and quantification shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: JMP dynamics are increased at sites where neutrophils transmigrate compared to sites where neutrophils migrate along the junction but do not exit.
claims.source: In line with the idea that neutrophils preferred JMPs, we found that JMP dynamics were increased at sites where neutrophils transmigrated compared to sites where neutrophils migrated along the junction but did not exit (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing JMP dynamics at different sites shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to initiate diapedesis by crawling towards a JMP of the neighboring endothelial cell.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that neutrophils preferred to initiate diapedesis by crawling towards a JMP of the neighboring endothelial cell. Consequently, the neutrophil used this JMP to exit and continued crawling underneath the endothelial cell that generated the JMP (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data showing neutrophil behavior at JMPs in Figure 2D and supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Once a neutrophil uses a JMP to cross the endothelium, other neutrophils follow this path and use the same exit-site.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed that once a neutrophil used a JMP to cross the endothelium, other neutrophils followed this path and used the same exit-site (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data showing sequential neutrophil transmigration at the same site in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Endothelial JMP dynamics increase at exit-sites after the first neutrophil crosses.
claims.source: This was in line with an increase in endothelial JMP dynamics at exit-sites after the first neutrophil crossed (Figure 2F), in line with a recent publication by Hyun et al., 2019.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased JMP dynamics after transmigration in Figure 2F and consistent with published findings.

claims.claim: Endothelial JMPs can function as exit-recognition sites that are reinforced by transmigration.
claims.source: These data suggest that endothelial JMPs can function as exit-recognition sites that are reinforced by transmigration.
claims.evidence: Conclusion inferred from observations that JMP dynamics increase after transmigration and subsequent neutrophils use the same sites.

claims.claim: VE-cadherin localizes at the basolateral area of JMPs but is not present on the actual JMP.
claims.source: To study the JMP phenotype in more detail, we used LLSM imaging and found that VE-cadherin localized at the basolateral area of JMPs but is not present on the actual JMP (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing VE-cadherin localization in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Junctional PECAM-1/CD31 is present on JMPs.
claims.source: In contrast, junctional PECAM-1/CD31 was present on JMPs (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing PECAM-1 localization on JMPs in Figure 3B and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: PECAM-1 covers at least 50% of the surface of the JMP.
claims.source: Using a 3D quantification algorithm, we found that PECAM-1 covered at least 50% of the surface of the JMP (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data from 3D analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions can be found in vivo in the cremaster muscle of mice.
claims.source: To examine whether JMPs are found in vivo and are correlated to TEM events, we used the cremaster muscle as a well-established in vivo model. The cremaster muscle of C57BL/6 mice were treated with TNF/IL1β and subsequently stained for PECAM-1 and neutrophil-specific coronin1 (Pick et al., 2017). We found that PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions can also be found in vivo, although we cannot quantify them as JMPs based on these images.
claims.evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data from cremaster muscle shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: PECAM-1 covers apical protrusions that surround adherent neutrophils in vivo.
claims.source: As with the in vitro data, PECAM-1 covered the apical protrusions that surrounded adherent neutrophils in vivo (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing PECAM-1 coverage around neutrophils in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: ACKR1 is expressed at CAAX-identified JMPs.
claims.source: To examine the location of ACKR1, we expressed an mNeonGreen-tagged variant of ACKR1 in HUVECs together with mScarlet-I-CAAX to label the membrane and cultured the cells in a mosaic manner to a full monolayer. We observed that ACKR1 is expressed at CAAX-identified JMPs (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that chemokines can be presented by JMPs.
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data showing ACKR1 localization at JMPs in Figure 3E and supplemental figures.

claims.claim: ICAM-1 localizes to JMPs.
claims.source: To identify the role of JMPs in the adhesion stage of TEM, we co-expressed ICAM-1 mScarlet-I and mNeonGreen-CAAX in HUVECs. Like ACKR1, ICAM-1 localized to JMPs (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data showing ICAM-1 localization at JMPs in Figure 3F and supplemental figures.

claims.claim: ICAM-1 and ACKR1 are not enriched at JMPs.
claims.source: Interestingly, when measuring the fluorescence at JMPs using a profile plot, we found that fluorescence of the proteins detected at JMPs increased to the same extend as the membrane marker CAAX (Figure 3—figure supplements 1B and D). Based on these data, we concluded that ICAM-1 and ACKR1 are not enriched at JMPs.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of fluorescence intensity showing proportional increase with membrane marker in supplemental figures.

claims.claim: JMPs may be involved in presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to crawling leukocytes.
claims.source: These results suggest that JMPs may be involved in two key steps of TEM. First by presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to the crawling leukocytes (Pruenster et al., 2009) and second, by presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for the leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
claims.evidence: Conclusion inferred from ACKR1 localization at JMPs and its known role in chemokine presentation, supported by citation.

claims.claim: JMPs may be involved in presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
claims.source: These results suggest that JMPs may be involved in two key steps of TEM. First by presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to the crawling leukocytes (Pruenster et al., 2009) and second, by presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for the leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
claims.evidence: Conclusion inferred from ICAM-1 localization at JMPs and its known role in leukocyte adhesion.

claims.claim: JMPs are rich in F-actin.
claims.source: To study the role of the actin cytoskeleton in JMPs, we used LifeAct-expressing endothelial cells and LLSM imaging, which revealed that JMPs are rich in F-actin (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing LifeAct signal at JMPs in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Actin-rich vascular structures that protrude apically are associated with TEM events in vivo.
claims.source: To investigate if these structures are also present in vivo, we used Lifeact-GFP knock-in mice (Fraccaroli et al., 2012) and studied the inflamed cremaster muscle vessel morphology. As Lifeact-EGFP is mainly expressed in the vascular endothelium and not in the leukocytes, allowing imaging of the endothelial actin cytoskeleton with excellent contrast (Fraccaroli et al., 2012), we used these mice to study the presence of luminal membrane protrusions. In vivo time lapse imaging showed actin-rich vascular structures that protruded apically and were associated with TEM events (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data from Lifeact-GFP mice showing actin-rich protrusions during TEM in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 reduces JMP dynamics.
claims.source: As the Arp2/3 complex is involved in actin nucleation, branching and lamellipodia formation (Goley and Welch, 2006), we hypothesized that its activity is required for the dynamics of JMPs. Indeed, treatment of endothelial cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 reduced JMP dynamics (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics after CK-666 treatment in Figure 4C-D.

claims.claim: Silencing Arp3 in endothelial cells results in reduced number of neutrophils that cross the endothelial monolayer under flow conditions.
claims.source: Therefore, we silenced Arp3 in endothelial cells using shRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 4—source data 1). Indeed, silencing Arp3, with two independent shRNAs, resulted in reduced number of neutrophils that crossed the endothelial monolayer under flow conditions (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced TEM events in Arp3-silenced cells in Figure 4E and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells silenced for Arp3 show reduced JMP dynamics.
claims.source: To specifically quantify membrane dynamics in Arp3-deficient endothelial cells, we co-expressed the Arp3 shRNA and mNeonGreen-CAAX from one plasmid, assuring that CAAX-expressing cells were indeed silenced for Arp3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E). Endothelial cells that were silenced for Arp3 showed reduced JMP dynamics (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics in Arp3-silenced cells in Figure 4F and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: Actin nucleation by the Arp2/3 complex is important for JMP formation and neutrophil TEM.
claims.source: These data underscore the importance of actin nucleation by the Arp2/3 complex for JMP formation and neutrophil TEM.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that Arp2/3 inhibition or silencing reduces both JMP dynamics and neutrophil TEM.

claims.claim: Rac1 inhibitor (EHT1864) reduces JMP dynamics.
claims.source: To test if Rac1 is required for JMPs, we used a Rac1 inhibitor (EHT1864) and found that JMP dynamics were reduced (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics after EHT1864 treatment in Figure 5A and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: JMPs display a significant increase in Rac1 activation.
claims.source: Next, we used FRET-based DORA Rac1 biosensor to measure Rac1 activity at JMPs (Timmerman et al., 2016; Timmerman et al., 2015). To this end, endothelial cells were transfected with the Rac1 biosensor and with mScarlet-I-CAAX. The FRET ratio was used as a read-out of Rac1 activity, and it was measured at JMP regions and compared with the average ratio at the full cell junctional region (for details see Materials and methods section). This analysis showed that JMPs displayed a significant increase in Rac1 activation (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET-based biosensor measurements showing increased Rac1 activity at JMPs in Figure 5B-C and supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to cross the endothelium at sites with high FRET ratio (high Rac1 activity).
claims.source: To correlate Rac1 activation with neutrophil diapedesis, we mapped the areas where neutrophils crossed the endothelium to the FRET ratio of the Rac1 biosensor. We found that neutrophils preferred to cross the endothelium at sites with high FRET ratio (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing neutrophils crossing at high Rac1 activity sites in Figure 5D-E and video.

claims.claim: No change in Rac1 activity is detected at regions where neutrophils adhere and crawl on the surface of the endothelium.
claims.source: However, no change in Rac1 activity was detected at regions where neutrophils adhered and crawled on the surface of the endothelium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the adhesion and lateral migration of neutrophils themselves did not trigger Rac1 activity in endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET measurements showing no change in Rac1 activity under crawling neutrophils in supplemental figures.

claims.claim: JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
claims.source: Together, these findings reveal that JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that Rac1 inhibition reduces JMP dynamics and that JMPs show increased Rac1 activity.

claims.claim: Local JMPs have an asymmetric phenotype at junction regions, with one cell generating the protrusion while the neighboring cell does not.
claims.source: At this point, the contribution of the two neighboring endothelial cells to the JMP is unclear. To study individual, neighboring endothelial cells in more detail, we mixed HUVECs expressing either mNeonGreen-CAAX or mScarlet-I-CAAX. Mosaic-like expression enabled us to distinguish individual endothelial cells that were adjacent to one another (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Interestingly, LLSM showed the presence of asymmetrical JMPs, meaning that one cell generated the protrusion, while the neighboring cell did not (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing asymmetric JMPs in mosaic-labeled cells in Figure 6A and supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Scanning electron microscopy confirms that JMPs display an asymmetric phenotype at endothelial cell-cell junction regions.
claims.source: Using scanning electron microscopy, we confirmed that JMPs displayed an asymmetric phenotype at endothelial cell-cell junction regions (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by scanning electron microscopy images showing asymmetric JMPs in Figure 6B and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: One endothelial cell shows higher JMP dynamics compared to the adjacent one at junction regions.
claims.source: To quantify this, we analyzed membrane dynamics at JMP regions using mosaic-expressing endothelial cells and found that one endothelial cell showed higher JMP dynamics compared to the adjacent one, as indicated by a ratio >1 (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing asymmetric JMP dynamics between adjacent cells in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The active Tiam1 mutant, C1199, activates endogenous Rac1 in endothelial cells.
claims.source: To further assess if local Rac1 activation can trigger the direction of neutrophil transmigration across an asymmetric junction, we overexpressed the Rac-specific RhoGEF Tiam1 in endothelial cells. Biochemical analysis showed that the active Tiam1 mutant, C1199, activated endogenous Rac1 in endothelial cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by biochemical Rac1 pulldown assay data shown in supplemental figure.

claims.claim: Tiam1-C1199 localizes at junctions as determined by VE-cadherin staining.
claims.source: Additional immunofluorescence imaging revealed that Tiam1 localized at junctions as determined by a perpendicular line scan across the cell-cell junction indicated by VE-cadherin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and line scan analysis shown in supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Tiam-C1199 recruits F-actin to junction sites.
claims.source: Similar line scan analysis showed that Tiam-C1199 recruited F-actin to these sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), in line with previous work by Lampugnani and co-workers (Lampugnani et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by line scan analysis showing increased F-actin at junctions in Tiam1-expressing cells in supplemental figure, consistent with published findings.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells expressing Tiam1-C1199 show increased F-actin content at junction regions.
claims.source: Where endothelial cells that expressed only control plasmids showed low levels of F-actin at junction regions, endothelial cells that showed asymmetric expression of Tiam1 (meaning one cell expressed Tiam1 and the adjacent cell did not) or both endothelial cells expressed Tiam1 showed increased F-actin content at junction regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of F-actin staining at junctions shown in supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Tiam1-C1199-induced junctional protrusions are approximately 2.5 µm in height.
claims.source: Tiam1-C1199-induced junctional protrusions were approximately 2.5 µm in height, as was determined by 3D imaging (Figure 6D) and were reduced in height upon treatment with the Rac1 inhibitor EHT1864 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D imaging measurements shown in Figure 6D and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to migrate underneath a Tiam1-C1199 expressing cell.
claims.source: When measuring the direction of migrating neutrophils that crossed the endothelium, we observed that neutrophils preferred to migrate underneath a Tiam1-C1199 cell (Figure 6E and Figure 6—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction shown in Figure 6E and video.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate underneath cells expressing constitutively active Rac1-Q61L.
claims.source: Similar results were found when expressing the constitutive active variant of Rac1, Rac1-Q61L, in a mosaic manner with control cells expressing LifeAct (Figure 6F and Figure 6—video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction in Rac1-Q61L expressing cells shown in Figure 6F and video.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate across junctions that display an asymmetric protrusion on one of the two neighboring endothelial cells.
claims.source: These data show that neutrophils prefer to transmigrate across junctions that display an asymmetric protrusion on one of the two neighboring endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with Tiam1-C1199 and Rac1-Q61L showing directional preference of neutrophil transmigration.

claims.claim: Neutrophils migrate from the top of an 'inactive' cell to underneath the 'active' protruding endothelial cell.
claims.source: As a result, neutrophils migrate from the top of an 'inactive' cell to underneath the 'active' protruding endothelial cell.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of neutrophil transmigration direction in asymmetric junctions.

claims.claim: Local activation of photoactivatable Rac1 induces local membrane protrusions.
claims.source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that local activation of Rac1, that is, one endothelial cell but not the neighboring one, triggers asymmetric JMPs that function as a local recognition site to drive diapedesis for neutrophils. To test this hypothesis, we used a genetically encoded photoactivatable Rac1 probe (Wu et al., 2009). By exciting the Lov2 domain, active Rac1 is released and induced local membrane protrusions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data showing membrane protrusions upon blue light activation of PA-Rac1 in supplemental figures.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate from the non-transfected cell underneath the PA-Rac1 expressing cell.
claims.source: We found that neutrophils preferred to transmigrate in the direction from the non-transfected cell underneath the PA-Rac1 expressing cell, in line with data presented above (Figure 6G and Figure 6—video 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction with PA-Rac1 shown in Figure 6G and video.

claims.claim: Local activation of the Rac1 probe increases the number of neutrophils that cross the endothelium.
claims.source: Moreover, local activation of the Rac1 probe increased the number of neutrophils that crossed the endothelium (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased TEM events upon PA-Rac1 activation in Figure 6H and supplemental figure.

claims.claim: Neutrophils prefer to exit the endothelium through junctions that display JMPs in an asymmetric manner.
claims.source: In summary, our data indicate that neutrophils preferred to exit the endothelium through junctions that display JMPs in an asymmetric manner, meaning that one endothelial cell exposes an apical protrusion and the other one does not (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing asymmetric JMPs and directional neutrophil transmigration.

claims.claim: Asymmetric JMP sites can be recognized as local endothelial TEM hotspots.
claims.source: These sites can be recognized as local endothelial TEM hotspots.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations that neutrophils preferentially use asymmetric JMP sites for transmigration.

claims.claim: Leukocytes use preferred exit sites during transmigration across the endothelium.
claims.source: Upon inflammation, leukocytes rapidly transmigrate across the endothelium to enter the inflamed tissue. Evidence accumulates that leukocytes use preferred exit sites, alhough it is not yet clear how these hotspots in the endothelium are defined and how they are recognized by the leukocyte.
claims.evidence: Statement based on accumulated evidence in the field, though specific mechanism was unclear prior to this study.

claims.claim: Leukocytes prefer endothelial membrane protrusions at cell junctions for transmigration.
claims.source: Using lattice light sheet microscopy, we discovered that leukocytes prefer endothelial membrane protrusions at cell junctions for transmigration.
claims.evidence: Main finding of the study supported by LLSM imaging and multiple experimental approaches.

claims.claim: Junctional membrane protrusions are present in an asymmetric manner, with one endothelial cell showing the protrusion and the adjacent one not.
claims.source: Phenotypically, these junctional membrane protrusions are present in an asymmetric manner, meaning that one endothelial cell shows the protrusion and the adjacent one does not.
claims.evidence: Key finding supported by LLSM and SEM imaging of mosaic-labeled endothelial cells.

claims.claim: Leukocytes cross the junction by migrating underneath the protruding endothelial cell.
claims.source: Consequently, leukocytes cross the junction by migrating underneath the protruding endothelial cell.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of neutrophil transmigration direction at asymmetric JMPs.

claims.claim: JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
claims.source: These protrusions depend on Rac1 activity and by using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe, we could artificially generate local exit-sites for leukocytes.
claims.evidence: Supported by experiments showing Rac1 inhibition reduces JMPs and PA-Rac1 activation induces JMPs and increases TEM.

claims.claim: Local induced junctional membrane protrusions facilitate/steer leukocyte escape/exit from inflamed vessel walls.
claims.source: Overall, we have discovered a new mechanism that uses local induced junctional membrane protrusions to facilitate/steer the leukocyte escape/exit from inflamed vessel walls.
claims.evidence: Overall conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Leukocyte transendothelial migration comprises leukocyte rolling, arrest, crawling, firm adhesion, and diapedesis.
claims.source: The current paradigm of leukocyte transendothelial migration (TEM) comprises leukocyte rolling, arrest, crawling, firm adhesion, and diapedesis (Alon and van Buul, 2017; Butcher, 1991; Muller, 2016; Nourshargh and Alon, 2014; Springer, 1994; Vestweber, 2015).
claims.evidence: Established paradigm in the field supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Diapedesis occurs either through the endothelial junctions (paracellular route) or through the endothelial cell body (transcellular route).
claims.source: The latter step occurs either through the endothelial junctions, known as the paracellular route or through the endothelial cell body, called the transcellular route (Carman, 2009; Wittchen, 2009).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claims.claim: Some locations favor the migration of multiple leukocytes that breach the endothelium in rapid succession.
claims.source: Interestingly, some locations seem to favor the migration of multiple leukocytes that breech the endothelium in rapid succession (Abtin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Observation from published literature cited.

claims.claim: Prior to exiting the circulation, leukocytes change their crawling morphology to a round appearance.
claims.source: Prior to exiting the circulation, leukocytes change their crawling morphology to a round appearance, indicating that at exit-sites differential and local regulation is required (Shulman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Observation from published literature cited.

claims.claim: What determines where leukocytes take the exit remains elusive.
claims.source: However, what determines where leukocytes take the exit remains elusive.
claims.evidence: Statement of the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

claims.claim: Perivascular macrophages can secrete chemokines that may cause local queues for neutrophil diapedesis in vivo.
claims.source: Recently, it has been shown that perivascular macrophages can secrete chemokines that may cause local queues for neutrophil diapedesis in vivo (Abtin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claims.claim: High surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration.
claims.source: For example, high surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration, while intermediate levels favor the paracellular route (Abadier et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2005), although the underlying mechanism is unclear.
claims.evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claims.claim: Intermediate levels of ICAM-1 favor the paracellular route of transmigration.
claims.source: For example, high surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration, while intermediate levels favor the paracellular route (Abadier et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2005), although the underlying mechanism is unclear.
claims.evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claims.claim: The endothelial actin cytoskeleton plays a dynamic role in controlling leukocyte TEM.
claims.source: Data from our lab (Heemskerk et al., 2016; Timmerman et al., 2016; van Buul et al., 2007; van Buul et al., 2010) and that of others (Adamson et al., 1999; Barreiro et al., 2002; Barreiro et al., 2008; Carman and Springer, 2004; Lyck and Enzmann, 2015; Muller, 2015; Vestweber, 2015) indicate a dynamic role for the endothelial actin cytoskeleton in controlling the factors described above.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on multiple studies from the authors' lab and others, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Two different hotspots exist during extravasation in vivo, one of which is located on the endothelium.
claims.source: Recently, Hyun and colleagues showed the existence of two different hotspots during extravasation in vivo (Hyun et al., 2019), one of which is located on the endothelium.
claims.evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claims.claim: Blocking actin polymerization of the endothelium prevents the leukocyte from properly adhering and spreading, and critically impairs leukocyte TEM.
claims.source: Perturbation of the endothelial actin cytoskeleton drastically influences the phenotype of the adherent leukocyte: blocking actin polymerization of the endothelium prevents the leukocyte to properly adhere and spread and consequently, leukocyte TEM is critically impaired (Barreiro et al., 2002; Carman et al., 2003; Carman and Springer, 2004; Schimmel et al., 2018; van Buul et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Finding from multiple published studies cited.

claims.claim: Once a leukocyte has adhered to the endothelium, F-actin is locally depolymerized underneath the adherent leukocyte.
claims.source: On the other hand, once a leukocyte has adhered to the endothelium, F-actin is locally (i.e. underneath the adherent leukocyte) depolymerized (Isac et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claims.claim: The endothelium can orchestrate local leukocyte diapedesis by remodeling its actin cytoskeleton at the subcellular level.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the endothelium can orchestrate local leukocyte diapedesis by remodeling its actin cytoskeleton at the subcellular level.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from findings about actin polymerization and depolymerization during TEM.

claims.claim: Leukocyte diapedesis is not a random event but occurs at predefined exit-sites.
claims.source: Our observations underscore that leukocyte diapedesis is not a random event but occurs at predefined exit-sites.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the authors' observations throughout the study.

claims.claim: Leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 seconds.
claims.source: As TEM is a very rapid process (leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 s), we used lattice light sheet microcopy, allowing high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity to monitor TEM in detail.
claims.evidence: Observation about the timescale of TEM that motivated the use of LLSM.

claims.claim: Lattice light sheet microscopy allows high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity.
claims.source: As TEM is a very rapid process (leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 s), we used lattice light sheet microcopy, allowing high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity to monitor TEM in detail.
claims.evidence: Description of the technical capabilities of LLSM.

claims.claim: JMPs express ACKR1, ICAM-1, and PECAM-1.

results.result: Under physiological flow conditions, most neutrophils transmigrate at the first junction they encounter, but only half do so immediately. Approximately 40% change direction during diapedesis, and neutrophils search for specific exit sites on the endothelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are supported by quantitative data from TEM under flow assays (Figure 1A-C) showing neutrophil behavior at junctions. The observations are consistent with prior work (Schenkel et al., 2004) and provide clear evidence that neutrophils exhibit complex migratory behavior when searching for transmigration sites.

results.result: Endothelial cells display junctional membrane protrusions (JMPs) that extend apically into the lumen, show dynamic appearance with various morphological shapes, and colocalize with VE-cadherin. TNFα treatment increases JMP volume and dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 are well-supported by LLSM imaging data (Figure 1D-H) showing JMP morphology, dynamics, and colocalization with VE-cadherin. The quantification of JMP volume and dynamics upon TNFα treatment provides robust evidence for inflammatory regulation of these structures.

results.result: JMP dynamics are consistently induced by various inflammatory stimuli (TNFα, LPS, IFNγ, IL1β) across endothelial cells from different origins. Short-term flow increases JMP activity while longer flow exposure reduces it to basal levels, with no directional preference. Inflammatory stimuli promote JMP dynamics but not their appearance or size.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 are supported by systematic quantification data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) comparing different inflammatory stimuli, endothelial cell origins, and flow conditions. The conclusion that inflammatory stimuli affect dynamics but not size/appearance is well-justified by the data presented.

results.result: Neutrophils preferentially transmigrate at sites with high JMP activity. JMP dynamics are increased at transmigration sites compared to sites where neutrophils crawl but don't exit. Neutrophils initiate diapedesis by crawling toward JMPs of neighboring cells, and subsequent neutrophils follow the same exit sites. JMP dynamics increase after the first neutrophil crosses, suggesting JMPs function as exit-recognition sites reinforced by transmigration.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including quantification of JMP dynamics at transmigration sites (Figure 2A-F), 3D imaging showing neutrophil behavior at JMPs, and observations of sequential neutrophil transmigration. The conclusion is consistent with published findings (Hyun et al., 2019).

results.result: VE-cadherin localizes at the basolateral area of JMPs but not on the actual protrusion, while PECAM-1 is present on JMPs covering at least 50% of their surface. PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions are found in vivo in mouse cremaster muscle and surround adherent neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are well-supported by LLSM imaging data (Figure 3A-D) showing differential localization of VE-cadherin and PECAM-1, quantification of PECAM-1 coverage (Figure 3C), and in vivo imaging from cremaster muscle. The in vivo data provides important validation of the in vitro findings.

results.result: ACKR1 and ICAM-1 localize to JMPs but are not enriched there relative to the membrane marker. JMPs may be involved in presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter and ICAM-1 for leukocyte integrin binding to initiate diapedesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by imaging data (Figure 3E-F, supplemental figures) showing ACKR1 and ICAM-1 localization at JMPs and quantification demonstrating proportional increase with membrane marker. Claims C30-C31 are reasonable inferences based on known functions of these molecules, though the functional role is not directly tested here.

results.result: JMPs are rich in F-actin and depend on Arp2/3 complex activity. Inhibition or silencing of Arp3 reduces both JMP dynamics and neutrophil TEM. Actin-rich vascular structures protruding apically are associated with TEM events in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 are strongly supported by LLSM imaging showing F-actin in JMPs (Figure 4A), in vivo imaging from Lifeact-GFP mice (Figure 4B), pharmacological inhibition data (Figure 4C-D), and genetic silencing experiments with two independent shRNAs (Figure 4E-F). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches provides robust evidence for the role of Arp2/3 in JMP formation and function.

results.result: JMPs depend on Rac1 activity. Rac1 inhibition reduces JMP dynamics, and JMPs display significantly increased Rac1 activation measured by FRET biosensor. Neutrophils prefer to cross the endothelium at sites with high Rac1 activity, but Rac1 activity does not change when neutrophils crawl on the endothelial surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are well-supported by pharmacological inhibition data (Figure 5A), FRET-based measurements of Rac1 activity at JMPs (Figure 5B-C), and correlation of transmigration sites with high Rac1 activity (Figure 5D-E). The finding that crawling neutrophils don't trigger Rac1 activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E) is important for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: JMPs display an asymmetric phenotype at junction regions, with one endothelial cell generating the protrusion while the neighboring cell does not. This asymmetry is confirmed by LLSM and scanning electron microscopy. Overexpression of active Tiam1-C1199 activates Rac1, localizes to junctions, recruits F-actin, and induces junctional protrusions approximately 2.5 μm in height.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 are strongly supported by multiple imaging modalities (LLSM, SEM) showing asymmetric JMPs (Figure 6A-C), biochemical validation of Tiam1-C1199 activating Rac1 (supplemental figure), and immunofluorescence showing Tiam1 localization and F-actin recruitment (supplemental figures). The convergence of structural and biochemical data provides robust evidence for asymmetric JMP formation.

results.result: Neutrophils preferentially migrate underneath endothelial cells expressing active Tiam1-C1199, Rac1-Q61L, or photoactivatable Rac1. Local activation of PA-Rac1 induces membrane protrusions and increases neutrophil transmigration. Neutrophils prefer to exit through junctions displaying asymmetric JMPs, migrating from the 'inactive' cell underneath the 'active' protruding cell. These asymmetric JMP sites function as local endothelial TEM hotspots.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C59 are exceptionally well-supported by multiple experimental approaches showing directional preference of neutrophil transmigration with Tiam1-C1199 (Figure 6E), Rac1-Q61L (Figure 6F), and PA-Rac1 (Figure 6G-H). The PA-Rac1 experiments are particularly compelling as they demonstrate causality by artificially generating exit sites on demand. This represents a major advance in understanding TEM hotspots.

results.result: The study discovers that leukocytes use preferred exit sites during transmigration, specifically endothelial membrane protrusions at cell junctions. These JMPs are present asymmetrically, with one endothelial cell showing the protrusion and the adjacent one not. Leukocytes cross junctions by migrating underneath the protruding cell. JMPs depend on Rac1 activity, and local induced JMPs facilitate leukocyte exit from inflamed vessel walls.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript, including LLSM imaging, functional assays, molecular characterization, and in vivo validation. The discovery of asymmetric JMPs as TEM hotspots represents a significant advance in understanding leukocyte extravasation.

results.result: JMPs are not induced by leukocytes themselves but through an intrinsic endothelial mechanism triggered by inflammatory signals like TNFα, which causes long-term Rac1 activation. Crawling leukocytes do not trigger JMP activity, dynamics, or localization, nor do they change endothelial Rac1 activity. Neutrophils continue crawling until encountering a JMP with high Rac1 activity. The regulation of JMPs is proposed to occur in a stochastic manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 are supported by experimental data showing no change in JMP dynamics or Rac1 activity with crawling neutrophils. Claims C107-C109 are reasonable inferences and hypotheses based on the observations, though C108-C109 represent speculative models rather than directly tested conclusions. The stochastic regulation hypothesis (C109) is supported by analogy to published findings but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Long-term flow conditions do not affect JMP dynamics or distribution, despite endothelial cells adjusting their morphology to flow by polarizing with increased Rac1 activity at the upstream side. The stochastic regulation of JMPs under inflammatory conditions is independent of flow direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C110 and C112 are supported by experimental data showing no directional preference of JMPs under flow (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). Claim C111 is established knowledge from cited literature. The finding that JMPs are flow-independent is somewhat surprising but well-documented.

results.result: JMPs are distinct from junction-associated intermittent lamellipodia (JAILs). JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension, while JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions, display trafficking molecules (ACKR1, ICAM-1, PECAM-1), and are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by the authors' data showing JMP characteristics (localization, molecular composition, regulation) and comparison with published literature on JAILs. The distinction is based on multiple differentiating features including localization, molecular composition, and regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: JMPs are found in vivo in mouse cremaster muscle. PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions surround adherent neutrophils in vivo, and actin-rich vascular structures that protrude apically are associated with TEM events in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims are supported by in vivo imaging data from cremaster muscle in C57BL/6 mice (Figure 3D) and Lifeact-GFP mice (Figure 4B). However, the authors acknowledge they cannot quantify these structures as JMPs based on the in vivo images alone. The in vivo validation is important but less definitive than the in vitro characterization.

results.result: Local activation of Rac1 using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe drives leukocyte exit on demand. PA-Rac1 activation induces local membrane protrusions, directs neutrophil transmigration underneath PA-Rac1 expressing cells, and increases the number of neutrophils crossing the endothelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C55-C57 are strongly supported by PA-Rac1 experiments (Figure 6G-H, supplemental figures) demonstrating that local Rac1 activation is sufficient to induce JMPs and direct neutrophil transmigration. This represents a key proof-of-concept that JMPs can be artificially generated to control TEM, with important implications for therapeutic applications.

results.result: JMPs offer new therapeutic targets to locally inhibit or enhance leukocyte extravasation. This mechanism may lead to novel strategies for immune cell therapies and targeting pathologies involving perturbed JMPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C100-C101, and C119 are speculative statements about potential therapeutic applications. While the PA-Rac1 experiments provide proof-of-concept for controlling TEM, no therapeutic validation is presented. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not supported by data in the current manuscript.

results.result: Background knowledge and literature context establishing the TEM paradigm, prior observations of TEM hotspots, roles of adhesion molecules and chemokines, and the involvement of the endothelial actin cytoskeleton in TEM.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C78, C87, C91-C94, C96-C99, C103, and C111 represent established knowledge from the field supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide necessary context for the study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the literature.

results.result: Summary statements about the study's main findings: leukocyte diapedesis occurs at predefined exit-sites, TEM is rapid (within 120 seconds), LLSM enables high-resolution imaging, JMPs express ACKR1/ICAM-1/PECAM-1, and a unique mechanism for paracellular TEM has been identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82, C90, and C118 are summary statements supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript. These represent valid conclusions drawn from the data, though they are restatements of findings already covered in other result groups.
